title: US proposes new tariffs on 14 trading partners, including China, Japan and the EU – as it happened
byline: Tom Ambrose, Graeme Wearden, Julia Kollewe, Sarah Butler, Lauren Aratani, Lisa O’Carroll, Jasper Jolly, Denis Campbell, Lauren Almeida
excerpt: New tariffs planned as Trump administration clamps down on ‘unfair trade practices’

US proposes new tariffs on 14 trading partners

Graeme Wearden

Newsflash: The Trump administration has proposed new tariffs on 14 major trading partners, including China, Japan and the European Union, according to reports.

The US Trade Representative’s office announced the duties after completing an eight-month Section 301 unfair trade practices probe into 16 trading partners, including close allies Japan, the European Union and South Korea, Reuters reports.

The move is designed to clamp down on ‘structural excess industrial capacity’.

A senior US official said that tariffs were proposed for goods from China, Bangladesh, Cambodia, the European Union, India, Indonesia, Japan, South Korea, Malaysia, Singapore, Switzerland, Taiwan, Thailand and Vietnam.

The specific rates are expected to be published in a US Federal Register notice later today.

The move follows the Supreme Court’s striking down of broader tariffs announced by President Trump.

Associated Press have more details of today’s move:

The legal basis of the planned tariffs is Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, which enables the U.S. government to investigate and retaliate against foreign trade practices that violate existing deals, are not justified by market forces or actively discriminate against American goods. A senior administration official told reporters that the new tariffs would be consistent with the trade deals that Trump reached last year with dozens of countries after threatening severe tariff hikes .

Brazil was singled out for extra punishment after talks on trade issues stalled, the official said. The U.S. is proposing higher import taxes for raw and refined sugar and a new 10% tariff on aircraft, a move that would hit Embraer, Brazil’s largest aircraft maker.

For some Chinese goods, the new 20% tariff will be stacked on top of other import taxes for a total rate of 45%.

Closing summary

That’s all from me, Tom Ambrose, and the business live blog for today. Thanks for following along.

Here is a round-up of the day’s main headlines:

  • The United States unveiled proposed tariffs on 14 economies including the European Union and China, after a months-long probe into alleged excess production – the latest move by US president Donald Trump to remake Washington’s trade relationships. The duties, proposed at up to 20%, come over allegations the economies “are promoting production and capacity divorced from the realities of demand and market principles,” a senior US official said on condition of anonymity.

  • The new levies target some of the largest US trading partners, including China, the European Union, India, Bangladesh, Cambodia, Indonesia, Japan, South Korea, Malaysia, Singapore, Switzerland, Taiwan, Thailand and Vietnam. The tariffs face a period of public comment before taking effect.

  • A 20% tariff is being proposed for China, the joint-highest for any economy, but US trade representative Jamieson Greer said the new levies were within the bounds of existing trade negotiations with Beijing. “China understands that we’re going to have some level of tariffs. This falls within that understanding,” he told US broadcaster CNBC on Wednesday, adding that the United States was also offering China exemptions on around $30bn of goods.

  • US partners like the EU, Korea and Taiwan, which have signed earlier trade deals, will see tariffs broadly capped at 15%. In a separate announcement, USTR also proposed additional tariffs on goods from Brazil, including aircraft, over alleged inaction on addressing US trade concerns.

  • The EU hit back at Donald Trump’s plans for more tariffs which come almost a year after his previous “liberation day” levies were struck down by the US supreme court. According to a statement by the US trade representative “the EU’s unreasonable acts, policies and practices” include “industrial plans to expand manufacturing”; policies to “promote production an exports”, “sustained market access barriers” and “preferential lending” to target domestic sectors.

  • The US economy grew at the fastest pace in three years in the quarter to September, while claims for unemployment benefits fell, according to official figures. GDP rose by an annualised 4.3% in the third quarter, revised up from the 3.4% reported last month, according to the US Bureau of Economic Analysis. Economists had forecast 3.5% growth.

  • In the UK, Poundland has called in administrators putting 12,000 jobs at risk ahead of Christmas after its owners rejected at least two last-ditch bids for the budget retailer. Administrators at AlixPartners have been appointed to the retailer, which has 600 stores in the UK and Ireland by Poundland’s directors. The chain is now expected to be broken up with significant job losses and store closures.

  • Amazon is planning to sell cars in the UK from early next year, in a move that threatens to disrupt the vehicle retail market. The Amazon Autos service will be launched in “early 2027”, starting with cars from Korean manufacturer Hyundai. It will be the first time the US company has sold cars outside its home country.

  • Eurostar cancelled some of its trains between London, Paris and Brussels today due to an “unexpected” strike. According to the Press Association, Eurostar is locked in annual pay negotiations with a union in France, where no decision has been made and talks are ongoing.

Thousands of Poundland workers face an uncertain future after the struggling retailer went into administration, putting 12,000 jobs at risk in the run-up to Christmas.

The retailer’s founder, Steve Smith, has warned that employees who lose their jobs could struggle to find new work for years, amid difficult conditions on Britain’s high streets.

We want to hear from people who work for Poundland about how they are feeling. How is the uncertainty affecting you and your colleagues? What would redundancy mean for you and your family?

We’d also like to hear from people working for Poundland suppliers, particularly those that rely on the retailer for most or all of their business. Are you worried about how the retailer’s administration could affect your job?

William Bain, head of trade policy at the British Chambers of Commerce, said the new US tariffs ought to “come as no surprise”.

He said:

President Trump’s administration had indicated it wanted to return effective tariff rates to their original 2025 levels, before they were struck down by the Supreme Court.

The UK was not involved in this investigation, and the Economic Prosperity Deal (EPD) we previously agreed, offers our companies a degree of protection from future tariff rises.

But there will still be concerns among UK businesses that Digital Services Taxes may form the basis of a future US trade investigation.

Bain added:

However, there is also good news for some UK exporters in today’s decision. They had lost a comparative edge over the EU and other countries due to the Supreme Court decision in February. Today’s announcement largely restores that.

But the tale of US tariffs is not over yet. The BCC wants to see full implementation of the EPD including lower tariffs for steel and aluminium exports as promised, and a pathway for lower tariffs across many other sectors of UK goods exports.

Poundland collapses into administration, putting 12,000 jobs at risk

Sarah Butler

Poundland has called in administrators putting 12,000 jobs at risk ahead of Christmas after its owners rejected at least two last-ditch bids for the budget retailer.

Administrators at AlixPartners have been appointed to the retailer, which has 600 stores in the UK and Ireland by Poundland’s directors. The chain is now expected to be broken up with significant job losses and store closures.

The retailer’s US owner, Gordon Brothers, which bought Poundland for a nominal £1 last year, has been under pressure to accept an offer that would save jobs and protect thousands of the retailer’s suppliers.

High inflation and heavy competition from budget stores, online specialists and supermarkets have left the 36-year-old retailer – the UK’s first and biggest nationwide single-price retailer – struggling.

The retailer’s board filed a notice of intention to appoint administrations last month – which was later extended – protecting Poundland from the demands of creditors until 26 November while a solution to its problems was sought.

Just two bidders interested in the whole company remained in talks right up until this week’s deadline.

Martin Property Group, a Northern Irish family-owned company, which has been working with the existing management, led by Barry Williams, for about two months, remained interested.

It was joined by a last-ditch bid from Germany’s Zachert Private Equity, a fund founded by a former Bloomberg journalist that specialises in acquiring mid-sized companies such as the German photo studio group Studioline and the US food and drink company Brands Within Reach.

Other bidders for the whole group included the little-known finance group Xyra Group Holdings, and the Irish investment company Innovest, which both fell out of the bidding race over the past week.

Donald Trump’s tariffs have contributed to higher prices for US consumers, and a Reuters/Ipsos opinion poll conducted after Republicans’ midterm losses found 62% of respondents supported efforts to ​repeal them.

But Trump has long vowed to ‌restore duties struck down by the US ​Supreme Court in February. The latest measures ​follow an eight-month investigation into unfair trade practices under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, Reuters reports.

US trade representative Jamieson Greer said the proposed tariffs would not apply to about $30bn of Chinese imports under consideration for tariff reductions through a bilateral mechanism known as the Board of Trade.

However, the new duties would be added to tariffs imposed on Chinese goods during Trump’s first term, which total roughly 25%.

They would not be imposed on top of the 10% and 12.5% tariffs introduced in July on a broader group of 60 trading partners over allegations of lax enforcement of anti-forced-labor laws.

Lauren Aratani

Tariffs have proven unpopular with US voters, who handed Democrats a decisive victory in the midterm elections that will give the party control of Congress. The Yale Budget Lab estimates that tariffs currently in effect have added an additional $900 in costs for each US household.

The rising cost of living was the number one issue for voters ahead of November’s midterm elections, according to a Harris poll survey for The Guardian. An earlier Harris poll found seven in 10 Americans blamed tariffs for higher prices.

Lisa O’Carroll

Donald Trump is keeping true to his threat of “obnoxious” tariffs, after the supreme court ruled that he had overstepped his legal authority in imposing his “liberation day” tariffs last spring, our colleague Lisa O’Carroll explains.

In this explainer we looked at the various backdoors available to him to reimpose tariffs, which he once described as his favourite term:

The 301 tariffs, which he is threatening to impose today, were considered the most “obnoxious” as they allow for unlimited tariffs to be imposed for four years against countries with unfair trade practices.

If applied to the EU today – and not challenged or overturned – they would hold until 25 November 2030, two years after Trump’s current term of office ends.

But the EU has already passed legislation including a sunset clause that would blow up the tariffs on 31 December 2029.

MEPs had originally sought a 2028 expiration date but pushed it back in negotiations with member states keen to keep Trump sweet.

“The latest US tariff announcement is not as alarming as it looks, with these new tariffs essentially replacing – rather than stacking on top of – the previously announced Section 301 tariffs related to forced labour concerns,” said Stephen Brown, chief North America economist at Capital Economics,

The increase in the effective tariff rate looks set to be a touch lower than we’ve been assuming for our forecasts, although the new tariffs will still provide a marginal boost to prices and keep core goods inflation firm into next year. Moreover, the US has left open the option of increasing tariffs if trade agreements – particularly with China – fall apart.

The USTR [United States Trade Representative] today confirmed its recommendations for tariffs under the Section 301 investigation relating to “Structural Excess Capacity and Production in Manufacturing Sectors”. Recall that the US administration has long suggested that it would use these latest Section 301 tariffs to bring the overall US tariff rate, based on 2024 import shares, up from close to 11% currently back toward the 14% that applied prior to the Supreme Court striking down the IEEPA [International Emergency Economic Powers Act] tariffs.

Yet to avoid overall tariff rates exceeding those already agreed with some countries, the USTR has proposed a framework in which these new tariffs – likely to take effect in early 2027 – will substitute for the prior Section 301 tariffs imposed under forced labour concerns, rather than stack on top of them. For example, China and Vietnam reportedly face the highest new tariff, of 20%, but those will replace the 12.5% Section 301 forced labour tariffs that China and Vietnam already faced. For the EU, a new 15% tariff replaces the prior 10% one. The other surprise is that Mexico will not face a new, higher tariff, perhaps because the USTR is content that its USMCA negotiations with the country are going well. (Canada was not subject to this investigation).

For now, the key message is that the additional tariff burden is likely to be small, especially as various goods are also not subject to these new tariffs, Brown said.

That said, note that the US has left open its ability to hike these tariffs if trade agreements fall apart. For example, the tariff on China could reportedly rise to 40% if negotiations break down, while the USTR’s reports give it flexibility to raise tariffs on other countries too. For example, the tariff ceiling on Vietnam is 35%, almost double the proposed tariff.

One final interesting point is that the USTR’s framework for substituting between these two different Section 301 tariffs means the US will be able to maintain the broadly agreed tariff rates on various trading partners even if the courts eventually strike one of the two sets of tariffs down. That lends some support to our view that the Trump administration’s tariffs will remain in place in some form for years to come.

Greer: a lot of this is baked in

US trade representative Jamieson Greer has claimed that these new tariffs shouldn’t rattle the global economy.

Speaking to CNBC, Greer says:

“We’ve talked to our trading partners about this — they know what we’re proposing.

“I think a lot of this is baked in, and I don’t think any of these would actually take effect earlier than a couple months from now.”

Sam North, market Analyst at the trading platform etoro, has looked at what the proposed fresh US tariffs might mean for the UK, if implemented. The UK is not on the list, but there could be knock-on effects.

Britain is being squeezed from three sides: energy, borrowing costs and now trade uncertainty. Fresh US tariff proposals arrive with markets already volatile, inflation rising and Ofgem announcing a 26% increase in the energy price cap from January. The Bank of England has already raised rates to 4% and left further increases on the table. Households risk paying more to heat their homes and service their debts simultaneously, leaving less money flowing into the wider economy.

The UK’s absence from Washington’s latest proposed tariff list offers some breathing space, although British businesses remain exposed through European supply chains and overseas customers.

A prolonged trade dispute could weaken export demand and delay investment, compounding the squeeze on spending at home. That sharpens the Bank’s dilemma, persistent inflation could demand further tightening just as trade tensions threaten growth. For UK investors, diversification and close attention to companies’ debt burdens and cash generation remain essential. Britain can escape the latest tariff list and still pay an economic price.

EU hits back at Trump's plans for more tariffs

Lisa O’Carroll

The EU has hit back at Donald Trump’s plans for more tariffs which come almost a year after his previous “liberation day” levies were struck down by the US supreme court.

Washington’s proposed new tariffs on 14 major trading partners including China, Japan, South Korea and the EU to combat what it calls structural excess industrial capacity, reviving global ‌trade tensions.

According to a statement by the US trade representative “the EU’s unreasonable acts, policies and practices” include “industrial plans to expand manufacturing”; policies to “promote production an exports”, “sustained market access barriers” and “preferential lending” to target domestic sectors.

These increase the US economic security risks especially in cars, chemicals and pharmaceuticals, it says.

The current tariff plan is to impose a 15% levy on EU imports, pegging it at the same level agreed with the EU and Trump’s course last July.

The EU said:

We will study the findings. At the same time we strongly reject the premise that Europe is a source of structural overcapacity. To the contrary, Europe is among those most exposed to overcapacity,” it said a possible reference to imports flooding in from China.

The EU and the US share a real concern about global overcapacity, much of it state-driven and concentrated in third countries. We regret the lack of joint action.

Nasdaq falls over 3% as AI sell-off gathers speed

Wall Street has opened lower, as the AI sell-off intensified, and investors digested new US tariff proposals and economic data.

The Dow Jones fell 780 points, or 1.56% to 49,238 while the tech-heavy Nasdaq dropped 791 points, or 3.3%, to 22,941 and the S&P 500 lost 165 points, or 2.3%, to 7,035 after the market open.

Matthew Ryan, head of market strategy at global financial services firm Ebury, said:

The US economy remains Teflon-coated, shrugging off elevated energy prices, rising Fed rates and AI-related jitters to post its strongest growth in three years in the third quarter. Resilient consumer demand and heavy AI capital expenditure are doing much of the heavy lifting, and we think they should remain a tailwind for US growth into 2027.

A sharp AI correction is admittedly a big risk to this momentum, though it is not our base case.

A print this strong makes it harder to argue against higher Fed rates, with the economy clearly robust enough to withstand further tightening. With core inflation above target and still rising, the question is no longer whether the Fed hikes again in December but how far it goes in 2027.

We still favour no change beyond December, but the risk of further hikes has clearly increased and that is keeping the dollar well bid.

New US tariffs proposed: what the experts say

These new proposed tariffs are ‘the last thing’ the market needs, when investors are already dealing with AI jitters, says Aneeka Gupta, director and equity strategist at Wisdomtree.

“The market is still dealing with the doubts that are being raised on further capex expansion plans by the tech space. And the last thing the market needed was to now see Trump rebuilding the tariff regime once again.”

“I think given the fact that the market’s focus really is on the tech ‌space, we aren’t seeing as big of a reaction.”

The big question is whether these tariffs last longer than previous levies which were blocked by the US courts.

Lee Hardman, senior currency analyst at Japanese bank MUFG, explains:

“From ​a market perspective it’s not ​that surprising and I don’t see it ​being a big market mover. The main market focus at the moment is ​on what’s happening in ‌AI-related investments.

The Trump ​administration finding an alternative ​way for the tariffs back in place, and as it’s replacing similar tariff rates it shouldn’t have a major effect on the inflation outlook. The next thing to watch is if these tariffs can stand the test of the time.“

US economy grows at fastest pace in three years

The US economy grew at the fastest pace in three years in the quarter to September, while claims for unemployment benefits fell, according to official figures.

GDP rose by an annualised 4.3% in the third quarter, revised up from the 3.4% reported last month, according to the US Bureau of Economic Analysis. Economists had forecast 3.5% growth.

Investment and consumer spending were stronger than previously thought, while government spending also rose, partly offset by a decline in exports.

Meanwhile, the number of people filing new claims for unemployment benefits in the US fell by 13,000 to 189,000 in the third week of November, well below market expectations of 200,000. It was the joint lowest figure in nearly six decades.

Continuing jobless claims, a gauge of outstanding unemployment, fell by 95,000 to 1,697,000 in the second week of the month, the lowest since 2023. This points to a resilient labour market.

The dollar rose by 0.13% against a basket of major currencies after the data. The pound fell 0.35% to $1.3067.

Stock futures extended losses, as the data bolstered expectations of a Federal Reserve interest rate hike in December.

The Fed’s preferred inflation gauge, the personal consumption expenditures (PCE) price index rose at an annual rate of 3.8% in October, matching analysts’ forecasts, while the core rate (which strips out volatile food and energy costs) was 3.3%, slightly higher than expected.

An official, who has briefed reporters about the plan, said that could push implementation into January, Reuters says.

The increase in the effective tariff rate looks set to be a touch lower than we’ve been assuming for our forecasts, although the new tariffs will still provide a marginal boost to prices and keep core goods inflation firm into next year. Moreover, the US has left open the option of increasing tariffs if trade agreements – particularly with China – fall apart.

The USTR [United States Trade Representative] today confirmed its recommendations for tariffs under the Section 301 investigation relating to “Structural Excess Capacity and Production in Manufacturing Sectors”. Recall that the US administration has long suggested that it would use these latest Section 301 tariffs to bring the overall US tariff rate, based on 2024 import shares, up from close to 11% currently back toward the 14% that applied prior to the Supreme Court striking down the IEEPA [International Emergency Economic Powers Act] tariffs.

Yet to avoid overall tariff rates exceeding those already agreed with some countries, the USTR has proposed a framework in which these new tariffs – likely to take effect in early 2027 – will substitute for the prior Section 301 tariffs imposed under forced labour concerns, rather than stack on top of them. For example, China and Vietnam reportedly face the highest new tariff, of 20%, but those will replace the 12.5% Section 301 forced labour tariffs that China and Vietnam already faced. For the EU, a new 15% tariff replaces the prior 10% one. The other surprise is that Mexico will not face a new, higher tariff, perhaps because the USTR is content that its USMCA negotiations with the country are going well. (Canada was not subject to this investigation).

For example, the tariff on China could reportedly rise to 40% if negotiations break down, while the USTR’s reports give it flexibility to raise tariffs on other countries too. For example, the tariff ceiling on Vietnam is 35%, almost double the proposed tariff.

Here is a round-up of the day’s main headlines:

  • The United States unveiled proposed tariffs on 14 economies including the European Union and China, after a months-long probe into alleged excess production – the latest move by US president Donald Trump to remake Washington’s trade relationships. The duties, proposed at up to 20%, come over allegations the economies “are promoting production and capacity divorced from the realities of demand and market principles,” a senior US official said on condition of anonymity.
  • The new levies target some of the largest US trading partners, including China, the European Union, India, Bangladesh, Cambodia, Indonesia, Japan, South Korea, Malaysia, Singapore, Switzerland, Taiwan, Thailand and Vietnam. The tariffs face a period of public comment before taking effect.
  • A 20% tariff is being proposed for China, the joint-highest for any economy, but US trade representative Jamieson Greer said the new levies were within the bounds of existing trade negotiations with Beijing. “China understands that we’re going to have some level of tariffs. This falls within that understanding,” he told US broadcaster CNBC on Wednesday, adding that the United States was also offering China exemptions on around $30bn of goods.
  • US partners like the EU, Korea and Taiwan, which have signed earlier trade deals, will see tariffs broadly capped at 15%. In a separate announcement, USTR also proposed additional tariffs on goods from Brazil, including aircraft, over alleged inaction on addressing US trade concerns.
  • The EU hit back at Donald Trump’s plans for more tariffs which come almost a year after his previous “liberation day” levies were struck down by the US supreme court. According to a statement by the US trade representative “the EU’s unreasonable acts, policies and practices” include “industrial plans to expand manufacturing”; policies to “promote production an exports”, “sustained market access barriers” and “preferential lending” to target domestic sectors.
